Where these hires go wrong

The role is brand new. The hiring process isn't.

The person running your hire has never built an AI team. They can check that the right words are on the CV. They can't tell whether the person behind it can actually do the job here, in your business. These are the six ways it goes wrong, and we've watched all of them.

Failure 01

The words are on the CV

Everyone lists AI agents, copilots and models now. A recruiter can confirm the words are there. Only someone who has built these systems can tell the difference between a project that went live and a slide deck about one.

Failure 02

You hire at the wrong level

A research-minded leader hired to deliver builds you an impressive lab you can't get anything out of. A hands-on builder hired to run governance has no authority when your auditor or your board starts asking questions.

Failure 03

Their experience doesn't transfer

They really did lead AI at a household name. They also had a 200-person platform team, clean data and an unlimited budget behind them. Take all of that away and many of them have never actually had to make it work.

Failure 04

The job description is someone else's

It gets copied from a tech giant's careers page, so it asks for research credentials you will never use, and misses the thing you actually need: someone who can get one useful thing working inside your company this year.

Failure 05

Nobody checks if anyone will use it

Most AI projects don't fail on the technology. They fail because the team on the floor carries on doing it the old way. Almost no interview process tests whether this person can win those people over.

Failure 06

You decide the reporting line last

The role gets buried two levels under IT with no budget and no seat at the table. Then the first ten real decisions, about team, tools and what not to build, get made by people who don't own the outcome.

The bit nobody says out loud

You've already had these thoughts. Here's what we'd tell you.

Every executive we speak to is sitting on one or two of these. Most people selling you something will talk around them, so here are straight answers.

Do we even need this hire yet?

Sometimes you don't. We've told clients to wait a quarter and sort out who owns the data first. We would rather tell you that than sell you a hire you're not ready for, because we'd like to be the people you call when you are.

Would I even know if they were bluffing?

Honestly, probably not, and that isn't a failing on your part. The vocabulary is about a year old and it changes every few months. Telling the difference is the one thing our experts are certain about, because they were building AI twenty years before any of these words existed.

Should we just promote someone internally?

Often, yes. Someone who already knows your business and has your team's trust starts with an advantage nobody external can buy. We'll assess your internal candidate against exactly the same scorecard and tell you honestly whether they're ready.

What if they leave after a year?

This is the real risk, and it usually isn't about money. AI leaders leave when the job was oversold or when they were given no authority to do it. Both of those get decided before the offer goes out, which is exactly when we're involved.

Are we about to badly overpay?

You might be. These salaries have moved fast and plenty of people are quoting numbers from the top of the market. We'll tell you what's actually being accepted right now, including when the figure you've been given is far too high.

Everyone tells me something different. Who do I believe?

Fair. Most AI advice comes from someone with a product to sell you at the end of it. Ours comes from people who have spent their own budget getting this wrong and then right, which is a much more expensive way to learn.
